lessons.title: PE, VC and Angel Investing: Power-Law Returns and the J-Curve

children.text: Info Edge, the company behind Naukri.com, backed a young food discovery startup called Zomato around 2010. When Zomato listed in 2021, that early bet was worth many times what Info Edge had put in. Stories like this are why so many Indian professionals now write cheques into startups and venture funds. What the stories leave out is the other side of the same asset class: the startups that shut down, the companies that raised at sky-high valuations and never recovered, and the funds that returned less than an index fund after ten years. Private equity, venture capital and angel investing do not have a normal risk-return profile. Their returns follow a power law, and their cash flows follow a J-curve. You need to understand both before the Zomato story means anything.

body.text: In venture and angel investing, most bets lose money and a tiny number of winners produce almost all the returns. The average outcome can look great while the typical investor's outcome is poor. Without enough bets, patience and access, you are more likely to get the typical outcome than the average.

children.text: The Power Law: Why Averages Mislead

markDefs.definition: A pattern in which a very small number of outcomes are enormously larger than all the rest, so a handful of results account for most of the total.

children.text: Listed stock returns cluster around an average. Early-stage startup returns follow a

. Global studies of venture deals have consistently found that roughly half to two-thirds of investments return less than the money put in, while a few percent return ten times or more and generate most of the gains. Here is a simplified, illustrative version of that distribution for angel investments.

body.title: What is the average bet worth?
body.prompt: Using the illustrative distribution above, calculate the expected money multiple of a single angel investment. Enter the multiple, for example 1.2.
body.explanation: 0 + 0.20 + 0.45 + 1.00 = 1.65x. Notice that the 5% of big winners contribute 1.00x, more than 60% of the total. If those companies take 7 years to exit, 1.65x works out to only about 7.4% a year, before fees, tax and the cost of illiquidity. That is roughly FD territory for startup-level risk.

children.text: Why the number of bets matters so much

With a 5% chance of a big winner in each deal, a portfolio of only a few startups will usually miss every winner. The chart shows the chance of holding at least one 20x winner as the number of investments grows.

children.text: These figures come from simulating many portfolios with the same illustrative distribution and equal cheques in each startup. Every portfolio has the same expected multiple of 1.65x, but an angel with five investments has a better-than-even chance of losing money overall. Only with 20 to 30 investments does the typical result start to look like the average. That requires real capital: 25 cheques of ₹5 lakh each is ₹1.25 crore, all locked away for the best part of a decade.

body.text: Access matters as much as luck. The most sought-after startups often raise from established funds and well-connected angels before retail platforms ever see them. Returns data from top-tier investors does not describe the deals most individual angels are offered.

children.text: The J-Curve: Losing Money Before Making It

markDefs.definition: The shape of a PE or VC fund investor's cumulative cash flows: negative in early years as capital is called and fees are paid, then rising as investments are sold and cash is distributed.

children.text: When you commit to a PE or VC fund, money goes out for years before much comes back. Fees are charged from day one, and early write-offs usually show up before the winners mature. Plot your cumulative cash flow and it traces the

body.title: Cumulative net cash flow on a ₹1 crore VC fund commitment (₹ lakh, illustrative)

body.caption: The same fund, year by year (₹ lakh, illustrative, net of fees)

children.text: This is a good fund: it doubles the money called and earns about 15% a year. Yet the investor is ₹80 lakh out of pocket at the end of year 4, is still behind at the end of year 7, and only moves into profit in year 8. Anyone who judges the fund, or needs the money, in the first half of its life sees only losses. And this illustration assumes the fund is a success. A below-median fund might never climb out of the curve.

body.text: The Chapter 2 risks all stack up here. Liquidity: close to zero for a decade. Valuation: interim values are estimates of unlisted companies. Manager risk: the gap between top and bottom VC funds is the widest of any asset class. Correlation: these are equity bets that often suffer when listed growth stocks fall, just with a lag.

children.text: Entry Price and Exit Route Decide Everything

A great company is not the same as a great investment. Paytm listed in November 2021 at an IPO price of ₹2,150 and fell about 27% on its first trading day, and it traded well below that price for years afterwards. Investors who came in at late-stage valuations, including many who bought unlisted shares before the IPO, lost money in a company that kept growing its business. Early investors in the same company did very well. The difference was the price paid, not the business.

body.title: Average vs typical
body.question: An angel platform says: "Our investors' deals have an average expected multiple of 3x." You plan to invest in 4 startups. Why might your likely outcome be much worse than 3x?
options: Because in a power-law distribution, a few big winners pull the average up, and with only 4 bets you will most likely miss them
Because platforms are not allowed to report returns
Because startup returns are normally distributed around the average
body.explanation: Power-law returns are dominated by rare, huge winners. With only 4 investments, the chance of holding one is low, so your most likely portfolio outcome is well below the average, and often below 1x.

body.title: Name the curve
body.textWithBlank: The pattern of negative cumulative cash flows in a fund's early years, followed by a recovery as investments are exited, is called the ___-curve.
body.explanation: The J-curve reflects early capital calls, fees and write-offs, followed by distributions as successful investments are sold. It is why judging a PE or VC fund in its first few years is misleading.

body.title: Rhea's angel plan
body.scenario: Rhea, a 33-year-old product lead at a Bengaluru fintech, has ₹30 lakh in savings and earns well. After a friend's startup was acquired, she wants to put ₹20 lakh into angel investments this year: ₹10 lakh each in two startups she likes on an angel platform. Her ESOPs in her employer are already worth about ₹25 lakh on paper.
body.prompt: Using the ideas in this lesson, explain the risks in Rhea's plan and suggest how she could approach angel investing more sensibly, if at all.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Too few bets. With only two startups, the chance of holding a big winner is low. Using this lesson's illustrative distribution, a portfolio of 2 would most likely return less than her money, even though the average looks attractive.

2. Too much of her wealth. ₹20 lakh is two-thirds of her savings, locked away for 7 to 10 years with no exit.

3. Hidden concentration. Her ESOPs are also an unlisted startup-style asset, and her salary depends on the same ecosystem. A funding winter could hit her job, her ESOPs and her angel bets together.

4. Access and selection. Deals available to her on a platform may not be the ones top funds compete for.

A more sensible approach:
- Keep an emergency fund and build a liquid core portfolio first.
- If she still wants angel exposure, limit it to a small share of her wealth, say 5 to 10%, that she can afford to lose completely.
- Spread it across many small cheques over several years, aiming for 15 to 25 or more companies, or consider a diversified VC fund.
- Treat her ESOPs as part of her startup allocation, not separate from it.

points: Angel, VC and PE share a lock-in but differ sharply in loss rates, time to exit and how wide the gap is between good and bad outcomes.
Startup returns follow a power law: most deals lose money and a few big winners create most of the gains.
In the illustration, the expected multiple is 1.65x, about 7.4% a year over 7 years, and more than 60% of that comes from 5% of deals.
Portfolio size is critical: an angel with 5 investments has about a 56% chance of losing money overall, falling to about 21% with 30.
PE and VC funds follow a J-curve: even a good fund can leave you ₹80 lakh down in year 4 on a ₹1 crore commitment and in profit only in year 8.
Entry valuation and exit route decide returns, so great companies can still be poor investments for late entrants, as Paytm's 2021 listing showed.
